It was run directly by the Impressionist painters themselves
practice.explain: The Salon was the dominant, state-sponsored exhibition that shaped which art was considered legitimate, generally favoring polished, traditional history paintings over the loose, everyday scenes Impressionists favored.

lessons.title: Cubism and the Break from Realism
lessons.intro: For roughly five hundred years, since Brunelleschi's mathematics, Western painting had mostly agreed that a picture should show an object from one fixed viewpoint. Early twentieth-century Cubism blew that agreement apart, showing multiple angles of an object at once on a single flat surface.

sections.heading: Picasso, Braque, and Multiple Viewpoints
body: Pablo Picasso's Les Demoiselles d'Avignon (1907), depicting five angular, fragmented female figures, is widely considered the rupture point that opened the door to Cubism, drawing influence from both Iberian sculpture and African masks that Picasso had encountered.

Working closely together, Picasso and Georges Braque developed Cubism through the years that followed: instead of depicting an object from one single, fixed viewpoint, as linear perspective had insisted upon since the Renaissance, Cubist paintings fracture an object into geometric facets that show several viewpoints of it simultaneously on one flat picture plane.

sections.heading: Analytic and Synthetic Cubism
body: The earlier phase, Analytic Cubism (roughly 1908 to 1912), broke objects down into a nearly monochromatic scaffold of overlapping planes, often to the point that the original subject becomes difficult to identify at a glance, prioritizing structural analysis of form over legibility or color.

Synthetic Cubism, developing after about 1912, moved in the opposite direction, reassembling images from simplified, flatter shapes and incorporating actual pasted materials, such as newspaper clippings or wallpaper, in collage, reintroducing brighter color and clearer, more legible forms.

example.problem: A Cubist still life shows a guitar's front view and side profile overlapping within the same fragmented image. Why does this violate the tradition of linear perspective that had governed Western painting since the Renaissance?
steps: Linear perspective is built on the rule of a single, fixed viewpoint: an object is drawn as it would look from one specific position and moment in time.

Showing the guitar's front and side simultaneously means the image is not depicting one fixed viewpoint at all, but multiple viewpoints of the same object fused together on one flat surface, directly rejecting that five-hundred-year-old convention.
example.answer: Cubism deliberately breaks with linear perspective's single-viewpoint rule by fusing multiple simultaneous viewpoints of an object into one fragmented, flattened image.

keyTerms.def: An early 20th-century movement fragmenting objects into geometric facets showing multiple viewpoints at once.
An early Cubist phase (c. 1908-1912) breaking objects into a near-monochromatic scaffold of overlapping planes.
A later Cubist phase (after c. 1912) reassembling flatter shapes and incorporating collage materials.
An artwork technique incorporating pasted materials, such as paper or fabric, directly onto the surface.

practice.q: What convention, standard in Western painting since the Renaissance, did Cubism directly reject?
choices: The use of oil paint
Depicting an object from a single, fixed viewpoint using linear perspective
The use of religious subject matter
Painting on canvas rather than panel
practice.explain: Cubism broke from linear perspective's core assumption that a picture shows an object from one single, fixed viewpoint, instead fusing multiple viewpoints into one fragmented image.

practice.q: What influences shaped Picasso's Les Demoiselles d'Avignon?
choices: Byzantine mosaics exclusively
Iberian sculpture and African masks
Japanese woodblock prints exclusively
Ancient Egyptian wall painting exclusively
practice.explain: Picasso drew on both Iberian sculpture and African masks he had encountered, influences visible in the angular, fragmented faces of the figures in Les Demoiselles d'Avignon.

practice.q: What distinguishes Synthetic Cubism from Analytic Cubism?
choices: Synthetic Cubism uses brighter color, flatter shapes, and incorporates collage materials
Synthetic Cubism came first and used only monochrome color
There is no meaningful difference between the two
Analytic Cubism incorporated pasted newspaper collage
practice.explain: Synthetic Cubism, developing after Analytic Cubism, reintroduced brighter color and flatter, more legible shapes, and incorporated actual pasted materials like newspaper in collage.

practice.q: What is the defining visual strategy of Cubism?
choices: Perfectly smooth, blended brushwork with no visible strokes
Fragmenting objects into geometric facets showing multiple viewpoints simultaneously
Depicting only landscapes with no human figures
Using exclusively religious iconography
practice.explain: Cubism's defining strategy is fracturing an object into geometric planes that represent several viewpoints of that object at once, rather than one single fixed perspective.

lessons.title: Contemporary Art Since 1945
lessons.intro: After the Second World War, the center of the art world shifted from Paris to New York, and the movements that followed increasingly abandoned any single shared style, splitting instead into competing, sometimes directly opposed, strategies for what art could even be.

sections.heading: Abstract Expressionism and Pop Art
body: Abstract Expressionism, centered in New York in the late 1940s and 1950s, emphasized process, scale, and raw emotional expression over any recognizable subject. Jackson Pollock's drip paintings, made by pouring and flinging paint onto canvas laid on the floor, prioritized the physical act of painting itself as much as the finished image, while Mark Rothko's large color-field paintings used soft-edged blocks of color to produce an immersive, meditative emotional effect.

Pop Art emerged in the 1960s as a direct reaction, embracing rather than rejecting mass media and consumer culture. Andy Warhol's screenprinted, mechanically repeated images of Campbell's soup cans and celebrities, and Roy Lichtenstein's paintings mimicking the look of mass-printed comic book panels, questioned the boundary between fine art and commercial, mass-produced imagery.

sections.heading: Pluralism in Recent Decades
body: Since the 1970s, art has increasingly resisted being described by any single dominant movement, diversifying instead into installation art (constructed environments viewers physically enter), performance art (art enacted live by the artist's body over time), video and digital media, and art incorporating global and previously marginalized perspectives once excluded from Western-centered art history.

This pluralism, many differing approaches coexisting rather than one style replacing another in sequence, is itself often treated as the defining feature of art since the 1970s, a significant shift from the earlier twentieth century's pattern of one avant-garde movement supplanting the last.

example.problem: Compare Jackson Pollock's drip technique to Andy Warhol's screenprint repetition as two different responses to twentieth-century mass media and individual expression. What is each artist emphasizing?
steps: Pollock's dripped, physical process foregrounds the individual artist's unrepeatable bodily gesture and raw emotional expression, resisting any sense of mechanical reproduction.

Warhol's screenprinting instead embraces mechanical repetition and the visual language of mass-produced consumer imagery, deliberately blurring the line between a unique fine-art object and an endlessly reproducible commercial image.
example.answer: Pollock's process emphasizes unrepeatable individual gesture and raw expression, while Warhol's screenprinting emphasizes mechanical repetition and mass media imagery, representing nearly opposite artistic responses to the mid-20th-century world.

keyTerms.def: A mid-20th-century New York movement emphasizing process, scale, and raw emotional expression over recognizable subjects.
A 1960s movement incorporating mass media and consumer imagery, associated with Warhol and Lichtenstein.
Art constructed as an environment or space that viewers physically enter or move through.
The coexistence of many differing artistic approaches, rather than one dominant style, especially since the 1970s.

practice.q: What did Jackson Pollock's drip painting technique emphasize?
choices: Precise, controlled realism
The physical process and gesture of painting itself
Mechanical reproduction of mass media imagery
Traditional religious iconography
practice.explain: Pollock's technique of pouring and flinging paint prioritized the physical, gestural act of painting as central to the work's meaning, not just the resulting image.

practice.q: What did Andy Warhol's screenprinted soup cans and celebrity images question?
choices: The value of abstract art
The boundary between fine art and mass-produced commercial imagery
The importance of color theory
The role of religion in art
practice.explain: Warhol's mechanically repeated screenprints of consumer products and celebrities deliberately blurred the line between unique fine art and mass-produced commercial imagery.

practice.q: What broad trend characterizes art since roughly the 1970s, according to most historians?
choices: A single dominant movement replacing all others
Pluralism: many differing approaches coexisting rather than one sequential dominant style
A complete return to Renaissance techniques
The disappearance of all figurative art
practice.explain: Since the 1970s, art has increasingly diversified into many coexisting approaches, including installation, performance, video, and global perspectives, rather than following one dominant sequential movement.

practice.q: Where did the center of the Western art world shift to after World War II, from its earlier home in Paris?
choices: London
New York
Berlin
Tokyo
practice.explain: After World War II, New York became the new center of the Western art world, hosting movements like Abstract Expressionism that had previously been centered in Paris.
